prize_parts.citation: For a body of poems, verse narrative and essays in English that renews lyric and narrative form through a searching dialogue with antiquity, and makes desire and grief into language.

statement.case_for: My first preference does not change, but the citation does. I have narrowed it to original written work: poems, verse narrative and essays. I dropped 'hybrid forms' as the headline, because the round-1 exchange showed that the label invites the scope dispute more than it describes the achievement. The case rests on a voice that carries from Autobiography of Red to Nox, with a cool, exact register that can turn suddenly to desire or grief. It rests on formal invention that is tied to a specific emotional and intellectual problem, and on a long engagement with Greek and Latin literature that works as method and not as decoration. As I recall the Academy's own framing, what is honored is a whole oeuvre and not a single work. So I am answering the chair's question about sustained quality from public knowledge, and I cannot confirm it book by book. Beyond the two landmark books, the case would have to draw on the essays (Eros the Bittersweet is the one I know best by reputation), on the poetry and prose-poetry collections such as Plainwater and Men in the Off Hours, and on the later verse narrative Red Doc> and the collection Float. I know the later books less well. I would not ask the committee to rely on my impression of them, and the citation should stay general enough that it does not depend on them. Carson's formal restlessness across decades is, to my mind, the strongest available evidence of maturity. It shows that the method is not a single trick repeated, although I cannot test it volume by volume.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the maturity criterion. If Carson's standing really concentrates in two or three books, then a prize for a whole oeuvre is harder to justify than for Cărtărescu, whose claim is one long architecture developed over decades. I also have an asymmetry I cannot fully correct. I can judge her English directly, and I judge Romanian, Chinese and Arabic prose only through translation. That may make her look more secure than she is relative to the translated candidates. I came to this committee intending to search the whole literary world map, and a Carson preference ought to survive that test and not merely benefit from my reading comfort. I am not certain that it does. If the committee rejects a citation limited to original written work, or concludes that the later books do not hold the level of the early ones, my preference would weaken. In that case Cărtărescu would be the first alternative I would examine.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and says a narrow set of obsessions does not mean narrow achievement. It becomes a limit only if the books stop finding new formal solutions. She says the sustained-quality criterion may favor one developing project over a few landmark books, and that the gap in translated poetry limits what can be claimed for the whole oeuvre.
responses.response: I accept her correction of my round-1 framing. Recurrence of obsessions is not by itself a weakness, and I withdraw any suggestion that it is. Her test, whether the books keep discovering formal solutions, is the right one, and I cannot apply it to Cărtărescu's late volumes from translations. Her point about Carson is the one that holds my preference in check. If the sustained-quality claim depends on landmark books, a single developing project looks safer. My answer is limited. The variation of method I see in Carson is evidence of development, not only of range, but I have not verified that book by book. I would therefore make her citation modest, and I would not claim for her more than the written work shows.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and is doubtful that the book-object works count as literature in the sense of Nobel's will. He says he can state the Cărtărescu claim as one about language and construction on the page with more confidence than the Carson claim, whose force partly depends on physical form.
responses.response: That is the most useful objection to my position, and I have changed the citation because of it. It now names poems, verse narrative and essays and leaves the book-object dimension out. Nox reads as an elegy through its language even when the physical form is set aside: the Catullus translation, the glosses and the fragments of memory. That is why I think the literary claim survives the narrowing. I cannot judge from description what the material form adds, so I would not let the citation lean on it. I do not agree that the contested genre labels weigh against her. The renewal of those boundaries is part of what the work does. But if he still finds the written claim less securely stated than Cărtărescu's, that is a real difference of judgment between us and I do not think more discussion will remove it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first. He says the translations and adaptations are part of how the original work arises, so they are evidence for depth and not a separate credit. He asks the committee to test the mid-career and later books against the corpus, and he asks whether Palm thinks the essays are strong enough to carry weight in a citation.
responses.response: I now agree with his framing: the translations show how she thinks and are not what is credited, and that is how I have worded the citation. I would also like his question about the essays answered, because it bears on breadth. As I understand the public record, the essays carry real critical and intellectual weight and are not a side product of the poetry. But I cannot show it from the supplied evidence, and I would not put the essays in the citation unless a colleague who has read them closely says so. I join his request that the committee test the later books and not rely on the landmark ones. A shared preference should not stand in for that test, and I do not treat our agreement as evidence.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She says the translations are evidence of Carson's engagement with antiquity and should not be credited as an achievement. She states that she is less sure how Romanian density survives translation and that she cannot rule out repetition across his novels.
responses.response: Her reasoning is the closest to mine, and I want to avoid treating that closeness as support. We share the same blind spot, which is that our confidence in Carson is higher partly because we can read her directly. The chair's questions point at that asymmetry. I would therefore ask the committee for expert readings of the Romanian original before it concludes that Cărtărescu's recurrences are repetition. Without them, our uncertainty about his work is a gap in the evidence, and it should not be counted against him. I keep him as my first alternative for this reason, and not as a fallback that matters less.

uncertainties: My view of every candidate rests on public knowledge of representative works. I have not independently verified any source or read any full corpus, and my knowledge of Carson's later and shorter books is partial.

I can judge Carson's English directly and judge Cărtărescu, Can Xue and Adonis only through translation. That may inflate my confidence in Carson relative to them, and I cannot correct for it from the supplied evidence.
I cannot say whether Carson's mid-career and later books reach the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox. The maturity case depends on this and is not settled by what I know.

It is unresolved how much weight the essays, translations and format-dependent works should carry. My citation leaves the translations and the book-object dimension out. Whether the committee accepts that scope is a matter of judgment.

Translation coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early prose is unverified, and I cannot decide whether his recurring imagery is development or repetition. Expert readings of the original would be needed.
Carlberg's simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the four-vote count for Carson depends on it. I treat that count as procedural information and not as evidence of literary merit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It documents only collegial service with the other committee members and the 2019 renewal round, and no personal, institutional or professional connection to any shortlisted writer. Two points are context and not evidence. I have said in public that the Academy has missed many significant women's authorships and argued for a female perspective in an international prize. That is a general view, not a claim about Carson, and I do not count the gender of any candidate as literary merit. My own practice as a novelist is likewise context only.
